---
title: "Cifra"
subtitle: "Codebook-driven text coding, validated against human coding"
---

## The problem

Social scientists — political science, sociology, geography — routinely turn
unstructured text into categorical data: is this news article describing a
protest? does this public statement support or oppose a policy? Historically
this is done by hand, with a research assistant reading each document and
filling in a spreadsheet against a codebook the researcher wrote.

LLMs can now automate a large share of that mechanical work. But every
researcher who tries currently reinvents the same pipeline from scratch —
and, more importantly, most skip the part that actually makes automated
coding trustworthy: checking whether the model followed *this specific*
codebook, or fell back on its own generic notion of the concept.

## What Cifra is

Cifra is a local-first tool: the researcher authors a codebook (a concept,
its categories, definitions, examples, boundary notes), points it at a text
corpus, and the software calls an LLM to fill in a structured results table —
one category, one rationale, one quoted evidence span per document. Every
result carries a full audit trail: the exact prompt sent, the raw response
received, which model and provider mode produced it.

It is **not** a manual qualitative-coding tool — [Taguette](https://www.taguette.org/),
[QualCoder](https://github.com/ccbogel/QualCoder), and
[QualiLab](https://github.com/luizpf42/QualiLab) already do that well. Cifra is
closer to the inverse: it automates the mechanical categorization step so a
human doesn't have to read every row, while treating the researcher's
judgment — codebook design, model/parameter choices, and the decision of
whether automated output is reliable enough to become research data — as
non-negotiable and non-automatable.

## What "automated" does not mean

Automation applies to one step: turning text into a category without a human
reading every row. It does not remove the researcher from anything else.
The researcher is still solely responsible for:

- **designing the codebook** — which categories exist, how each is defined,
  where the conceptual boundaries sit;
- **choosing the pipeline** — which corpus, which model, which provider;
- **interpreting results**; and
- **deciding, via validation, whether automated coding is reliable enough
  to use as data.**

The Codebook Editor is the most important screen in the software, not a
form to get through before "the real part."

## Why validation is not a footnote

[Halterman & Keith (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.10747) — and the
same group's 2026 follow-up — show that off-the-shelf LLMs frequently
ignore a codebook's specific operationalization and substitute their own
generic notion of a concept instead: including a labor strike under
"protest" even when the codebook explicitly excludes it, for example. A
model that looks fluent is not the same as a model that followed the
instructions.

Cifra ran this failure mode for real, not hypothetically. See
[Why Validation Matters](validation.qmd) for the numbers: an under-specified
codebook produced results with essentially zero discriminating power on a
third of a real test batch, and a hypothesis's own scope condition got
silently ignored. Enriching the codebook — not switching models — fixed
both, and the before/after is verifiable, not just asserted.

## Current status

Cifra is pre-1.0, under active development. As of this page:

- **Corpus import** — CSV/XLSX/pasted text, with column mapping.
- **Codebook editor** — structured form with a live YAML preview.
- **Runs** — kick off an extraction against a corpus + codebook, watch it
  progress, pick API-key mode (schema enforced via
  [`instructor`](https://github.com/jxnl/instructor)) or CLI mode
  (any installed CLI the researcher already has a subscription for).
- **Results** — browsable table, inline edits, CSV/XLSX/JSON export, and a
  per-run [GUIDE-LLM](https://llm-checklist.com/)-shaped AI-use disclosure
  report.
- **Validation** — gold-label import (including round-tripping with
  QualiLab), Cohen's kappa, precision/recall/F1 per category.

See [How It Works](how-it-works.qmd) for the pipeline end to end, and
[Architecture](architecture.qmd) for the technical design and why it looks
the way it does.

Source, issues, and full history: [github.com/mancano-tales/cifra-text-as-data](https://github.com/mancano-tales/cifra-text-as-data).
